title: Baptism
lead: Baptism is the washing with water by which people enter the Christian church, "into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). Almost all Christians practice it, but they differ on what it does, who should receive it, and how it should be done.

sections.h: Washing and new beginnings in the Old Testament
sections.b: The law of Moses used washing with water to make people clean before God (Leviticus 15:5–13; Numbers 19:17–19). Naaman was healed of his skin disease when he dipped seven times in the Jordan (2 Kings 5:14). Ezekiel promised that God would sprinkle clean water on his people and give them a new heart (Ezekiel 36:25–27). The New Testament reads several stories as pictures of baptism: the flood that carried Noah's family through the water (1 Peter 3:20–21), Israel passing through the sea (1 Corinthians 10:1–2), and circumcision, the sign of the covenant given to Abraham's family (Genesis 17:10–12; Colossians 2:11–12).
sections.refs: Leviticus 15:5–13; Numbers 19:17–19; 2 Kings 5:14; Ezekiel 36:25–27; 1 Peter 3:20–21; 1 Corinthians 10:1–2; Genesis 17:10–12; Colossians 2:11–12

sections.b: John the Baptist called people to be baptized as a sign of repentance, and Jesus was baptized by him in the Jordan (Mark 1:4–11). The risen Jesus sent his followers to make disciples and baptize them (Matthew 28:19). On the day of Pentecost Peter told the crowd to repent and be baptized for the forgiveness of sins (Acts 2:38). In Acts, people are baptized soon after they believe, sometimes whole households at once (Acts 8:36–38; Acts 16:15, 33; 1 Corinthians 1:16). Paul says that in baptism believers are buried with Christ and raised to new life (Romans 6:3–4), and Titus 3:5 speaks of "the washing of rebirth." Jesus told Nicodemus that a person must be born of water and the Spirit (John 3:5). The Greek baptizō means to dip or wash.
sections.refs: Mark 1:4–11; Matthew 28:19; Acts 2:38; Acts 8:36–38; Acts 16:15–33; 1 Corinthians 1:16; Romans 6:3–4; Titus 3:5; John 3:5

sections.b: Catholic and Orthodox teaching holds that baptism washes away sin and gives new birth by the Holy Spirit; it is the door to the other sacraments. Lutherans also teach that God works through baptism to forgive sins and give faith, because the water is joined to God's word. Reformed, Anglican and Methodist churches call baptism a sign and seal of God's covenant promise, a means of grace, though they say it does not save apart from faith. Baptists, many Pentecostals and most evangelical free churches call it an ordinance: an act of obedience in which a believer who is already saved shows faith in public. Churches of Christ and other Restorationist churches teach that a believer is baptized for the forgiveness of sins (Acts 2:38). Quakers do not practice outward baptism, holding that the true baptism is the inward work of the Spirit.
sections.refs: Acts 2:38; Romans 6:3–4; Titus 3:5; 1 Peter 3:21; Galatians 3:27; Matthew 3:11

sections.b: Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican and Methodist churches baptize the infants of believing parents. They point to the household baptisms in Acts, to Peter's promise that "belongs to you, and to your children" (Acts 2:39), and to circumcision on the eighth day (Genesis 17:12). Baptists, Anabaptists, Pentecostals and many others baptize only people old enough to confess faith, since the New Testament links baptism with repentance and belief (Acts 8:36–37); they often dedicate infants instead, as Hannah gave Samuel to the LORD (1 Samuel 1:27–28). Churches also differ on the method. Orthodox churches immerse three times; Baptists insist on full immersion; many others pour or sprinkle water. The Didache, an early Christian manual, already allows pouring when there is not enough water.

common: Most churches accept one another's baptism when it is done with water in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.
uncommon: Quakers and the Salvation Army do not practice water baptism at all.
